It provided scenarios in which this reduction happened over 1, 2.06, 3 and 4 years. The EAG agreed with the company's approach and used the 5‑year period in its own updated base case. The committee assessed the validity of the 5‑year period. It recalled that median PFS in ECHO was 72.5 months in the acalabrutinib arm and 47.8 months in the placebo arm. It thought that 5 years (60 months) may be an underestimate for how long the progressed-disease utility would take to decrease to 0.45. It also noted that increasing the length of time to reach 0.45 increased the ICER. The committee accepted that its preference to apply time-dependent progressed-disease HSUV from the time of health-state entry was not possible. It acknowledged that the company's and EAG's preferred approach does not account for people entering the health state at later time points, which caused uncertainty. The committee also requested further analysis to determine the external validity of 0.45 as a progressed-disease HSUV, with alternative sources explored. This was not provided by the company during consultation, so uncertainty remained about the validity of this value. The committee concluded that the company's approach to modelling progressed-disease HSUV in its updated base case was uncertain but appropriate for decision making in the absence of more reliable data or a more flexible model structure.

headline: Subsequent treatment durations
text: The company applied subsequent treatment costs as a one-off cost for people whose disease progressed in each cycle. The cost was calculated from the number of PFS events in each cycle, multiplied by the proportion of PFS events that were non-fatal, and the proportion of people with progressed disease who had subsequent treatment. One-off costs were applied based on the distribution of subsequent treatment options and time on treatment. In the company's submission, the duration of subsequent treatments was modelled based on the time on treatment from a variety of sources. The EAG noted that the company used a variety of approaches for calculating subsequent treatment durations, including using median PFS data from relevant studies for R-BAC and VR-CAP. The EAG was concerned that using PFS data may overestimate subsequent treatment duration, because some people in the progression-free state would stop treatment before progression. The EAG preferred to calculate subsequent treatment durations by using mean estimates of treatment durations when possible. The EAG assumed chemotherapy treatments would be given for a maximum 6 cycles, which is consistent with R-CHOP treatment when it is used at first line. During consultation, the company updated its base case to match the EAG's approach. The committee concluded that this was appropriate for decision making.

headline: Second-line subsequent treatment distributions
text: The company determined second-line subsequent treatment distributions based on clinical expert opinion. It explained that distributions from ECHO did not represent UK clinical practice. The committee noted that based on the company's clinical expert opinion (obtained before TA1081 was published), 100% of people who had BR at first line would have ibrutinib if they had a second-line treatment. The Cancer Drugs Fund lead confirmed that since TA1081 was published, people would likely have zanubrutinib rather than ibrutinib (see section 3.2 ). The clinical expert noted that after first-line treatment with acalabrutinib plus BR, R-CHOP would be the only viable second-line treatment option. During consultation, the company updated its model so that all people having second-line treatment after BR had zanubrutinib. It also updated its model so that all people having second-line treatment after acalabrutinib plus BR had R-CHOP. The EAG agreed that the company's approach was reasonable for the base-case analysis. The committee concluded that it was appropriate to assume all people who had BR first line would have zanubrutinib if they had second-line treatment. It also concluded it was appropriate to assume all people who had acalabrutinib plus BR at first line would have R-CHOP if they had second-line treatment.

headline: Including third-line subsequent treatments
text: The company included third-line subsequent treatments, including CAR-T therapies, in its base-case analysis. It did a post-hoc analysis of time to next treatment 2 (TTNT2) to help understand the impact of treatment sequencing. TTNT2 was defined as the time from randomisation to third-line treatment after randomised treatment was stopped, or death. The results showed a 24% reduction in risk (hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.98) of needing third-line treatment after acalabrutinib plus BR compared with placebo plus BR for the ECHO ITT analysis set. The company argued that these results showed that subsequent treatment was needed less often and later with acalabrutinib plus BR, reflecting better disease control. It stated that the TTNT2 analysis reduced the uncertainty of model inputs associated with subsequent treatments and supported including third-line treatments in the base-case results. The EAG acknowledged the observed reduction of people needing third-line treatments after acalabrutinib plus BR. But it was uncertain whether this represented a delay in treatment need driven by longer PFS, or absolute effect that would continue indefinitely over the modelled time horizon. The EAG thought the difference in proportions of people having third-line treatments between the 2 ECHO trial arms was highly uncertain. It was also uncertain about whether the difference represented UK clinical practice. So, the EAG removed third-line subsequent treatments from its base-case analysis. It noted that this approach would avoid capturing the costs of third-line subsequent treatments without capturing OS benefits. The clinical expert confirmed that there are no routine third-line treatment options for MCL, other than CAR-T therapy (brexucabtagene autoleucel) for those who are eligible. The committee noted that brexucabtagene autoleucel is currently only available through the Cancer Drugs Fund; see TA677. Section 2.2.15 of NICE's manual on technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance says that technologies recommended with managed access are not considered established practice in the NHS. The committee acknowledged the relevance of TA677 to this appraisal, and noted that it is currently being reviewed. It noted that there are no well-established third-line treatment options for MCL other than brexucabtagene autoleucel, which is not routinely commissioned. The committee noted that removing third-line treatments from the economic model would reduce uncertainty caused by the limitations of the PSM (see section 3.5 ). During consultation, the company updated its model to remove third-line subsequent treatments. The committee concluded that it was appropriate to exclude third-line subsequent treatments from the model.

headline: Acceptable ICER
text: NICE's manual on technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance notes that, above a most plausible ICER of £25,000 per QALY gained, judgements about the acceptability of a technology as an effective use of NHS resources will take into account the degree of certainty around the ICER. The committee will be more cautious about recommending a technology if it is less certain about the ICERs presented. But it will also take into account other aspects including uncaptured health benefits. The committee noted the high level of uncertainty, specifically that: the OS data was immature and no statistically significant OS benefit was shown for acalabrutinib plus BR (see section 3.3 ) the ECHO trial was not fully generalisable to NHS clinical practice and may overestimate absolute survival (see section 3.4 ) the economic model structure was uncertain because the results were not validated using a Markov model (see section 3.5 ) the SMR of 1.09 was uncertain because of a lack of evidence for this value in people with MCL treated at first line (see section 3.7 ) progressed-disease HSUV was not applied at the time of health-state entry because of the PSM model structure (see section 3.9 ) the validity of the minimum value of progressed-disease HSUV was not explored (see section 3.9). The committee concluded that an acceptable ICER would be towards the lower end of the range NICE considers a cost-effective use of NHS resources (£25,000 to £35,000 per QALY gained).

headline: Cost-effectiveness estimate
text: The committee's preferred assumptions aligned with the company's updated base case, and include: BR as the only relevant comparator for people with untreated MCL who are not eligible for an autologous stem cell transplant (see section 3.2 ) using the ITT population in the model (see section 3.6 ) applying an SMR of 1.09 to the background mortality (see section 3.7 ) using the generalised gamma distribution to extrapolate PFS (see section 3.8 ) using the log-normal distribution to extrapolate OS (see section 3.8) decreasing progressed-disease HSUV from 0.787 at model entry to 0.45 over a 5‑year period (see section 3.9 ) subsequent treatment durations calculated using mean estimates of treatment durations when possible and limiting chemotherapies to 6 cycles (see section 3.10 ) all people who have BR first line have zanubrutinib if they have second-line treatment (see section 3.11 ) all people who have acalabrutinib plus BR at first line have R-CHOP if they have second-line treatment (see section 3.11) third-line treatments are not included in the model (see section 3.12 ). The cost-effectiveness results include confidential prices for comparator treatments, so the exact results cannot be reported here. Using the committee's preferred assumptions, the committee concluded that the ICER for this evaluation is in the acceptable range.

headline: Equality
text: The committee did not identify any equality issues, and none were raised by the company or other stakeholders during the appraisal or during consultation.

headline: Uncaptured benefits
text: The committee considered whether there were any uncaptured benefits of acalabrutinib plus BR. It did not identify any additional benefits not captured in the economic modelling. So, the committee concluded that all additional benefits of acalabrutinib plus BR had already been taken into account.

headline: Recommendation
text: Using the committee's preferred assumptions, the cost-effectiveness estimates are within what it considers a cost-effective use of NHS resources. So acalabrutinib plus BR can be used, within its marketing authorisation, as an option for untreated MCL in adults who are not eligible for an autologous stem cell transplant.
